text: dsh-nonead-ursim 是面向 DSH Web 客户端的 Universal Robots 机器人控制与仿真插件。它注册机器人工具，并在 DSH 右侧栏提供实时 3D 数字孪生面板。主要能力包括关节与笛卡尔运动、状态和位姿读取、离线运动学仿真，以及通过推送遥测更新的机器人视图。适合需要在 DSH 中连接机器人控制工具或先用虚拟机器人演练动作的开发与操作场景。运行需要 Python 及 numpy、paramiko；默认使用本地仿真。

dsh-nonead-ursim adds Universal Robots tools and a live 3D panel to DSH's web client. It supports joint and Cartesian motion, pose and status reads, and local kinematics simulation. The view follows robot telemetry. Requires Python, numpy and paramiko; simulation is the default.
想让 DSH 里的 AI 控制一台 Universal Robots 机械臂。
有没有办法在 DSH 里先模拟 UR 机械臂的运动？
让 DSH 展示机器人当前关节姿态和 TCP 位姿。
我想在 DSH 侧栏看 UR 机械臂的 3D 数字孪生。
能不能让机器人按关节角或笛卡尔坐标移动？
需要一个能读取机器人状态、型号和姿态的 DSH 工具。
I want DSH tools to move a Universal Robots arm by joint or Cartesian targets.
Can I inspect a robot's pose and status in a live 3D view inside DSH?
dsh-nonead-ursim 的功能「机器人运动控制」：通过 DSH 工具向 UR 机器人发送关节或笛卡尔运动目标，并支持查询关节与 TCP 位姿。调用时提供目标机器人地址和相应运动参数。
dsh-nonead-ursim 的功能「离线仿真」：创建虚拟 UR 机器人并在本地按运动学更新姿态，可用工具启动、停止或读取仿真状态。无需先连接真实控制器。
dsh-nonead-ursim 的功能「3D 数字孪生面板」：在 DSH 右侧栏挂载机器人视图，使用状态流呈现关节姿态和 TCP 信息，并提供面板控制入口。
dsh-nonead-ursim 的功能「连续遥测视图」：worker 推送机器人关节和 TCP 数据，面板读取最新缓存并在状态变旧时回退读取，避免只依赖命令队列轮询。

dsh-nonead-ursim README · dsh-nonead-ursim：**A DeepSeek Harness (DSH) plugin that lets you control Universal Robots (UR) collaborative arms directly from natural language, developed by Suzhou Nonead Robot Technology Co., Ltd. based on the same logic as the company's own nUR MCP Server.** ([Suzhou Nonead Robot Technology Co., Ltd.](https://www.nonead.com))

dsh-nonead-ursim README · dsh-nonead-ursim：This plugin shares the same ancestry as the company's `Nonead-Universal-Robots-MCP` (see "Reference implementation" below). It exposes the "control a UR robot with AI" capability as **native DSH tools**: the plugin starts a persistent Python worker (which internally reuses the vendored `URBasic` library), and tools talk to the robot through that worker. After a single `connect`, you can keep issuing commands to the same IP.

dsh-nonead-ursim README · dsh-nonead-ursim：> 🧪 **Simulation-only by default (since 0.1.0).** This plugin drives **an offline, kinematics-level virtual UR robot** on the reserved loopback address `127.0.0.1` — and, unless you ask for more, nothing else. **In the default `motionMode: 'sim'` it has no real-robot channel at all**: a real IP is rejected as invalid input (`SIM_BADARG`) before anything is dispatched, and the vendored `URBasic` RTDE / Dashboard / SSH paths are unreachable from the tool surface. A real-robot channel **can** be enabled explicitly since 0.1.4 (`motionMode: 'real'` plus an allow-list — see *Real-robot channel (off by default)* below); the default above is unchanged by that. There is no `connect`-to-a-robot step: The simulation is started for you on demand (`UR12e`, upright pose, 100 % scaling), so the plugin works with **no real robot anywhere in the picture**. Commands that need a real controller (force mode, safety bits, programs, raw script, conveyor, power/brakes/freedrive) keep their tool names but answer honestly with `SIM_UNSUPPORTED` — they never fall through to a robot. Standard/tool I/O and the registers *do* have a simulation meaning since 0.1.5: an

dsh-nonead-ursim README · Overview：`dsh-nonead-ursim` gives a DSH agent a **Universal Robots arm it can drive in plain language** — the
complete tool surface of a UR controller (89 `ursim_*` tools: joint and Cartesian motion,
multi-segment continuous sequences, OptiMove,
drawing primitives, pose and status readback, RTDE telemetry, standard/tool I/O and registers,
URScript, TCP/payload/tool settings, force mode, conveyor tracking), plus a live **3D simulation
panel** that renders the same joint data those tools read.

dsh-nonead-ursim README · Overview：Out of the box it drives an **offline, kinematics-level virtual UR robot** on the reserved loopback
address `127.0.0.1`: no hardware, no real controller, nothing to install beyond Python — start a
simulation and issue commands. A real controller is addressed only after you ask for it explicitly
(`motionMode: 'real'` plus a `realRobotIps` allow-list), and the motion approval gate is **off by
default** (since 0.2.3; set `requireApprovalForMotion: true` to turn it on).

dsh-nonead-ursim README · Overview：What the simulation models and what it does not is a deliberate, stated boundary: **motion is real
kinematics**; **telemetry is estimated** and labelled as such; **I/O and registers are in-memory
state**; anything that genuinely needs a controller (force mode, safety-status bits, program load and
execution, raw scripts, conveyor) answers `SIM_UNSUPPORTED` instead of pretending. It is **not** a
safety-assessment tool — there is no dynamics and no safety function — so cycle time, collision and
safety-distance questions stay outside its scope.

dsh-nonead-ursim README · Feature overview：Every tool except `ursim_ping` takes an `ip` argument. **A `connect` first is not required** for the
simulation target: it comes up on demand (`ursim_sim_start`, or automatically on the first motion
addressed to the reserved loopback address). A real controller is out of reach until you enable the
real-robot channel in the configuration — see *Real-robot channel (off by default)* below.

dsh-nonead-ursim README · Read-only 3D digital simulation：The plugin also ships a **read-only 3D digital simulation** of the robot, rendered with three.js: the entry is a card in the **right sidebar's Start panel**, directly below the "Workspace files / New terminal / Browser" cards, and selecting it fills the right sidebar's content area with the live 3D view. The view subscribes to the host's **SSE stream** (`/twin/stream`, one frame every 100 ms), so it stays in sync with the live robot's **joint poses, tool (TCP) coordinate frame and recent motion trajectory**. The simulation is **strictly read-only — it never sends a command to the robot**: it only subscribes to the host's read-only routes and renders what it receives. A toolbar offers a reset-view control plus isometric / front / side / top presets, and the camera and base grid are framed from the model's bounding box, so a UR3 and a UR20 are both framed correctly — **except while the "Reach" layer is on, where framing switches to an absolute reference** (the largest built-in model's reach bound) so every model is drawn against **one ruler**: the UR3 envelope (≈0.80 m) takes ~37 % of the view while the UR20's (≈2.17 m) fills

dsh-nonead-ursim README · Read-only 3D digital simulation：**Telemetry is pushed, not polled.** The worker pushes readings at 20 Hz and every panel frame reads that push cache first, so the view keeps updating **while the robot moves** — the single-threaded command queue that motion confirmation occupies is never touched. Only a stale (>300 ms) or missing cache falls back to an explicit read, and panel reads use a dedicated **2.5 s budget with `killOnTimeout:false`**: a read-only visualisation read must never destroy the robot session (RTDE/Dashboard) just because it was busy. If a stall does happen, the stream still emits `stale` events and the panel writes "data stopped updating N s · retrying" rather than leaving a silently frozen arm on screen; after a disconnect it reconnects with exponential backoff (capped at 30 s). Set `DSH_URSIM_TWIN_PUSH=0` to turn the push channel off for comparison.

dsh-nonead-ursim README · Read-only 3D digital simulation：**A swapped robot swaps the model.** The model is cached per IP **together with the connection epoch it was read under**, so a different robot at the same IP is detected and the client reloads the mesh, **drops the previous robot's interpolated sample pair and trajectory** (otherwise the new arm slides over from the old pose and the trajectory line connects two robots' TCPs with a move that never happened), re-frames the camera from the new bounding box and updates the reach envelope and joint limits. Failed loads retry on a 3 s throttle instead of leaving the old arm on screen forever. ⚠️ Detection takes up to the vendored 30 s data-stall timeout, during which the panel still shows the last reading (old model, old pose); call `ursim_connect` again to correct it immediately.

dsh-nonead-ursim README · Read-only 3D digital simulation：**Offline simulation in the panel.** The panel's top row carries an "offline simulation" control: one switch plus three selectors — **model**, **start pose**, **speed scaling**. **Opening the panel now starts a simulation by itself, with `UR12e` / upright pose / 100 %** — real robot connected or not — so the simulation is useful the moment the card is expanded. The AI then drives the model right there: motion tools act on a **kinematics virtual robot** at `127.0.0.1`, the picture really moves, and **no real robot receives a single byte**. If a simulation is already running (started by the AI through `ursim_sim_start`, or by another window) the panel **adopts that one and never rebuilds it** — rebuilding would push the virtual robot back to its start pose. Collapsing the panel **stops** the simulation and returns the data source to automatic resolution. The simulated state is flagged three times over, because a moving simulated arm looks exactly like a real one: a purple **SIMULATION badge** in the view's top-left corner, a status line reading "Offline simulation · UR12e", and **"offline simulation (not a real robot)" in the

dsh-nonead-ursim README · Read-only 3D digital simulation：**The host self-heals the simulation — and the memory survives a restart.** `SIMS` lives in the Python child's memory, so once that child is replaced (crash restart, plugin reload, process reaped) the virtual robot is gone. The host therefore **remembers the simulation configuration** and confirms the robot is still there before handing a simulated command to the worker (immediately when the child generation changed, otherwise once every 10 s as a fallback); if it is gone it rebuilds it from that memory and logs the fact — never leaving the contradiction of "switch on, every command reports not connected". An explicitly stopped simulation is **not** resurrected, and the rebuild happens once: a run of motions does not repeat the probe. A rebuild puts the virtual robot **back at its start pose** (that is the cost, and the log says so).

dsh-nonead-ursim README · Read-only 3D digital simulation：That memory used to be process-local, so a **host** restart (reopening DSH, reloading the plugin) lost it and the self-healing had nothing to heal from. It is now written to disk (`persistSimState`, default on; `<DSH_HOME>/plugin-data/dsh-nonead-ursim/sim-state.json`, overridable with `simStateFile`): what is persisted is the **intent** (`enabled`), not the last picture — stopping a simulation writes `enabled: false`, so a stopped simulation stays stopped across restarts, while one that was running is created again on load with the same model, start pose and speed scaling (the log says so, and the panel shows why if that restore fails). Persistence is a bonus: a read-only data directory or a corrupt file degrades to "no memory" with one warning, never a failed start.

dsh-nonead-ursim README · Read-only 3D digital simulation：**The simulation's capability boundary is code, not a documentation promise.** It implements **kinematics only** — forward/inverse kinematics, joint and Cartesian trajectory interpolation, pose readback. The motion tools (`movej`/`movel`/`movep`/`movec`/`run_sequence`/`servoj`/`move_optimized`/`move_x|y|z`/`move_tool_*`/`draw_*`/`wait_steady`/`stopj`/`stopl`) and the readback (`get_joint_pose`/`get_tcp_pose`/`get_robot_model`/`status`/`get_target_values` and friends) all work; **every other command reports `SIM_UNSUPPORTED`** (force mode, RTDE telemetry, safety-status bits, program load/execution, raw scripts, I/O, registers, conveyor, power/brakes/freedrive) together with a pointer to URSim for the real thing — it would rather say "not here" than return a plausible-looking result. The forward kinematics is **element-wise identical** to the client's `fk.js` (`test/sim-backend.test.mjs` pins it), so a read-back TCP always agrees with where the picture draws it.

dsh-nonead-ursim README · Read-only 3D digital simulation：**The panel follows the app's colour theme.** Light / dark / system is DSH's own appearance setting: the theme plugin projects the resolved snapshot onto the document as the boolean `body[data-ds-dark-theme]` attribute plus the `--dsw-alias-*` design tokens. The panel therefore colours itself **from those tokens** (falling back to theme-paired local values only when the host tokens are absent, e.g. a bare preview page), so it follows the setting — and any third-party theme that overrides aliases via `ctx.theme` — with **no JavaScript involved**. The one thing CSS cannot reach is the WebGL base grid, whose colours are baked into the geometry's vertex colours: `src/client/theme.js` watches the same signal and `scene.js`'s `applyTheme()` repaints the grid **in place** (no geometry rebuild, no new `GridHelper`), so switching the theme never disturbs the camera, the model or the recorded trajectory.

dsh-nonead-ursim README · Read-only 3D digital simulation：**The panel speaks eight languages and follows the app's own.** Simplified Chinese, English, Japanese, Spanish, French, German, Russian and Brazilian Portuguese (`pt-BR` shares the `pt` dictionary the app uses). The language is not guessed: the app's locale service writes the active language into `<html lang>` (`zh` becomes `zh-CN`, every other id as-is), the panel reads that first and only then falls back to `__DSH_LOCALE__` and `navigator.language`, defaulting to Chinese for anything unrecognised (a Chinese user must never be silently downgraded to English). Switching needs **no reload**: copy goes through `liveStrings()`, which re-resolves the current `<html lang>` on every access, so the next render is already in the new language. Each language carries 143 keys, all eight key sets are symmetric, and `test/strings.test.mjs` pins it.

dsh-nonead-ursim README · Read-only 3D digital simulation：**Six things the panel shows that the tools alone cannot.** Since 0.1.8 the top-left badge is a
**three-state mode indicator**, not just a simulation watermark: purple `SIMULATION` while a virtual
robot is being driven, red **`REAL MODE · <allowed IPs>`** whenever `motionMode: 'real'` is configured
(shown even while disconnected — "no badge" must never read as "safe", and an empty allow-list says so
explicitly), and a neutral `NOT CONNECTED` when nothing is driving anything. The telemetry rows gained
the two readings that were already being delivered but never drawn (joint currents, TCP speed) and are
suffixed **`(estimated)`** whenever the host marks them `telemetry_estimated` — the panel must not
present an estimate in the same shape as a measurement. The capability boundary is readable in the
panel itself: a collapsible line under the simulation controls lists how many ops each bucket holds,
with the full list in its tooltip. And since 0.1.9 there is an **I/O and registers** block: expand it to
read the 16 digital outputs, the 16 digital inputs and both analog inputs (bits rendered as
`00000000 00000001` — the standard an

dsh-nonead-ursim README · Read-only 3D digital simulation：| Route | Description |
|---|---|
| `GET /nonead-ursim/twin/stream[?ip=<ip>]` | **SSE stream** (what the client uses by default): one full state frame every 100 ms, plus `stale` (this frame's read has not returned yet) and `frame-error` (this frame failed) events |
| `GET /nonead-ursim/twin/state[?ip=<ip>][&detail=1][&io=1][&reg=int|double|bit&from=0&count=8]` | Live pose (joint angles / TCP / model). `detail=1` adds the dashboard-side state (safety mode, run state, speed scaling, joint temperatures/currents); `io=1` adds the 16 digital outputs, 16 digital inputs and both analog inputs; `reg=<set>&from=&count=` adds one **slice** of registers (`count` capped at 16 — they are per-index getters). The pose channel keeps polling independently: a failing `detail`, `io` or `reg` query never takes it down, it only writes `{error}` into its own field |
| `GET /nonead-ursim/twin/asset?model=<urXX>` | GLB mesh, with a content-hash `ETag` + `immutable` and `If-None-Match` → 304 support |
| `GET /nonead-ursim/twin/models` | The model list actually present locally |
| `GET /nonead-ursim/twin/sim` | Current offline-simulation state (on/of

dsh-nonead-ursim README · Read-only 3D digital simulation：Failure responses carry a **machine-readable `code`** (e.g. `no_robot` / `robot_not_connected` / `ambiguous_robot` / `worker_unavailable` / `robot_error`) and echo the resolved `ip`, so the UI can say which of four very different failures happened (it used to render one "not connected" line for all of them). A read that is only **temporarily** unavailable (most often: the worker is busy executing a motion command) is *not* reported as `robot_error`: the host replays the last known reading with `stale:true` (for up to 30 s), so the simulation keeps its picture and says the data is stale.

dsh-nonead-ursim README · Option 1 — install from npm (recommended)：The plugin is published on npm as `dsh-nonead-ursim` ([npmjs.com/package/dsh-nonead-ursim](https://www.npmjs.com/package/dsh-nonead-ursim); `latest` is **0.3.12**). One command installs it into the target profile:

```sh
dsh plugin --profile web add dsh-nonead-ursim

Restart DSH afterwards. `cordis.patch.yml` inserts the plugin line automatically and the tools appear as `ursim_*`. Pin a version with `dsh-nonead-ursim@0.3.12` when you need one.

dsh-nonead-ursim README · Python runtime：The plugin needs a usable Python and a few dependencies (`numpy`, `paramiko`) to start the worker. Point it at an interpreter with the `pythonBin` config:

```sh
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

dsh-nonead-ursim README · Python runtime：`pythonBin` (default `python`), `commandTimeoutMs` (motion/script timeout, default `60000`), and `connectTimeoutMs` (first-connect timeout, default `30000`) in `cordis.patch.yml` can all be overridden per deployment. If `python` is not on PATH, use an absolute path, e.g. `"C:\\Python312\\python.exe"` or `"/usr/bin/python3"`.

dsh-nonead-ursim README · Python runtime：> ⚠️ **The dependencies must be installed for the interpreter the worker actually uses (a real trap)**
> `lib/worker.js` points `PYTHONPATH` at the plugin's `python/` directory, and CPython imports
> `sitecustomize.py` from there at startup if it exists. This repository once carried a
> **machine-local** `python/sitecustomize.py` that hardcoded a user-level `site-packages` path into
> `sys.path` — so it worked on that one machine, while on any other machine, or from a published
> install (the file is **not** in the `files` list), `import numpy` fails outright and every tool call
> dies. The correct setup is to **install the dependencies for the interpreter `pythonBin` points at**
> (or point it at a venv). `ursim_ping` / `npm run test:python` is the self-check for that chain, and
> `npm run verify:host` validates tool registration through the host's real schema DSL (it should
> report 89/89).

dsh-nonead-ursim README · Health check / testing：Verify the plugin and Python runtime without touching a real robot:

```sh
npm run test:python   # python ur_worker.py --selfcheck: verify Python/numpy/paramiko/URBasic/RTDE config
npm test              # run all 49 test files AND every check gate (see below), then summarise
npm run test:node     # Node-side only: skips the test files *and* the gates that need Python
npm run check         # all static + cross-language gates without running the test files

dsh-nonead-ursim README · Health check / testing：- **49 test files** under `test/` (e2e protocol self-check, approval gate, simulation routes, client
  state machine, FK, vendored-library regressions) — enumerated from `test/test-manifest.json`
  (Python-dependent 17 / Node-only 32), which `check:manifest` keeps honest so a Python-using file can
  never be silently unlisted.
- **11 check gates**: `check-test-manifest` / `check-package-metadata` / `check-client-bundle` /
  `check-doc-tools` / `tool-matrix` / `check-doc-links` (Node) and `check-worker-ops` /
  `check-tool-params` / `check-rtde-recipe` / `check-approval-gate` / `check-new-ops` (Python). When
  the interpreter has no `numpy`, the Python-dependent items are reported as **SKIP with the reason**,
  never as a pass. `check-tool-params` compares the tool schema against the Python handler on both
  sides by *parsing* them (the snapshot that carries `op` for every tool, and `ast` for the handler),
  so parameter names, required-ness and types are all cross-checked.

(49 test files + 11 gates, 0 failed / 0 skipped); `npm run verify:host` against the running host
(`dsh` / `dsh-tools` 0.2.2-alpha.3, `cordis` 4.0.6-alpha.2, `schemastery` 3.18.6-alpha.2) reports

dsh-nonead-ursim README · Health check / testing：It checks the peer ranges against the installed versions, compiles **every** tool parameter schema with the host's real value-schema DSL (a rejected schema silently drops that tool), drives the host route registration, and validates the `dsh.client` declaration plus the client bundle's `__ModuleLoader__` id. Exit code `0` means this plugin works with that host. Against the current host (`@deepseek-ai/dsh` / `dsh-tools` **0.2.2-alpha.3**, `cordis` **4.0.6-alpha.2**, `schemastery` **3.18.6-alpha.2**) it reports **4/4 peer checks and 89/89 tools registered**.

dsh-nonead-ursim README · Health check / testing：Both install layouts are handled. A packaged host keeps its modules in `resources/app.asar`, which plain Node cannot read, so the script re-executes itself through the host's own executable with `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1` — the runtime the plugin actually loads in; when the well-known install locations miss, it scans the drives (this machine installs to `D:\Software\Nonead DSH Desktop`). If no host is found it falls back to the repository's own dev copy of `@deepseek-ai/dsh-tools` and **says so explicitly**, rather than quietly reporting a green result for the wrong host.

dsh-nonead-ursim README · Health check / testing：Supported host ranges — every one of them is kept, none is replaced: `dsh` / `dsh-tools` `0.1.2-rc.1` → `0.2.2-alpha.3`, `cordis` `4.0.2` → `4.0.6-alpha.2`, `schemastery` `3.18.2` → `3.18.6-alpha.2`. When a new host jumps to a new prerelease family, add **one comparator for that family** to both `package.json` and the root `peerDependencies` of `package-lock.json` (semver only lets a prerelease version match a range containing a comparator with the same `major.minor.patch` tuple), then add the version to `test/host-peer-matrix.test.mjs`, which fails if any supported family loses its comparator or if the two files disagree.

dsh-nonead-ursim README · How it works：```
DSH model        @deepseek-ai/dsh-tools        python/ur_worker.py          UR robot
  │  ursim_movej(...)  │                              │                          │
  ├────────────────►  ctx.tools.register(defineTool)                        │
  │                  │  lib/worker.js               │                          │

dsh-nonead-ursim README · How it works：- **`python/ur_worker.py`** — a persistent stdio JSON worker. It keeps `ROBOTS` / `ROBOT_MODELS` dicts, connects by IP, and runs one command per call. Motion commands use (bounded) "arrival confirmation" polling and return a structured error on failure.
- **`lib/worker.js`** — lazily starts the worker once and keeps it alive, matching line-delimited JSON requests/responses, with timeout and cancel (forwards `exec.signal`).
- **`lib/index.js`** — the Cordis plugin that imports `defineTool` to register the above as tools; `inject: ['tools']`.

dsh-nonead-ursim README · Tool naming & examples：Tool names are stable as `ursim_*`. Example prompts:

> Connect to 192.168.1.199 and read the current TCP pose.

```
ursim_connect(ip="192.168.1.199")
ursim_get_tcp_pose(ip="192.168.1.199")
```

> Lower the TCP of 192.168.1.199 by 20mm along the Z axis.

```
ursim_get_tcp_pose(ip="192.168.1.199")
ursim_move_z(ip="192.168.1.199", distance=-0.02)
```

> Draw a circle of radius 50mm (vertical plane).

```
ursim_draw_circle(ip="192.168.1.199", center=[0.3,-0.2,0.4,0,3.14,0], r=0.05)
```

dsh-nonead-ursim README · Notes / limitations：- **Connection persistence** — the worker process lives for the plugin's lifetime and keeps robot connections by IP; after a worker crash or a DSH restart you must `connect` again.
- **Remote control mode** — some UR robots must be in "remote control" before they execute motion/program commands, and `ursim_connect` reports that state. **CB3 robots running URSoftware 3.1 through 3.20 already allow remote control by default (nothing to enable at the settings level)**; a `remote_control: false` reading still means the controller is *currently* not in remote mode — in local/teach-pendant mode URScript and motion commands are silently discarded, so switch the pendant to remote control. Other firmware (e-Series, or CB3 outside that range) needs Remote Control enabled in PolyScope first. `ursim_get_status` also reports `remote_control_raw`, and an unreadable state is reported as unknown rather than pretended to be `false`.
- **Tool digital I/O** — `ursim_get_digital_in` / `ursim_set_digital_out` with `which="tool"` control the tool-flange digital I/O. Tool digital signals are **not carried by RTDE**, so reading a tool input runs a short URScri

dsh-nonead-ursim README · Real-robot channel (off by default)：This release *can* drive a real controller, but only when you explicitly ask for it:

```yaml
motionMode: 'real'               # default 'sim' — nothing else can reach a real robot
realRobotIps: '192.168.1.10'     # comma-separated allow-list; empty ⇒ every target is refused
```

dsh-nonead-ursim README · Real-robot channel (off by default)：- **`sim` (the default) is a structural guarantee, not a policy.** The worker rejects any address
  other than the reserved loopback one *before* dispatching, so the RTDE / Dashboard / SSH /
  remote-control code is unreachable — not "present but unused".
- **`real` additionally requires the allow-list.** A target outside `realRobotIps` is refused on the
  host side before it reaches the worker; an empty list refuses everything (fail-closed), and the
  plugin logs a warning if you enable `real` without writing one.
- **The simulation stays available in both modes**, and the reserved loopback address *always* means
  the virtual robot — it is never handed to the real-robot implementation. (Otherwise forwarding a
  controller's port to loopback would be a way back in.)
- **With the gate turned on there is no approval exemption in `real` mode**: every gated command asks
  a human, including commands aimed at the simulation (with the gate off they all pass). That also
  closes the audit's H-2 finding — the exemption used to be host-side state that the model itself
